turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Friday, the ninth of October. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
The haze doubled overnight while the official forecast stayed on the same three words it has used since Sunday.
[curious] Two French ministries counted the same arrested teenagers and came out a thousand apart.
And a country that ran out of dollars in April is dredging new land to sell.
[excited] That last one. I've been thinking about it since five this morning.
It closes the book. Start at home, though — the air.
Give me the numbers.
At five this morning every region of the island was Unhealthy. Central a hundred and fifty-six, West a hundred and fifty-two, South and East both a hundred and thirty-one, North a hundred and seven.
That's the daily index. What did the hourly one do?
That's the story. Yesterday afternoon the highest hourly reading on the island sat at eighty-seven, at two o'clock and again at three. We printed that yesterday as a plateau.
And it wasn't.

It held for two hours, then rose in every hour but one for the next eleven. Ninety-eight, a hundred and four, a hundred and thirteen, a hundred and twenty-eight, a hundred and forty-five, a hundred and fifty-one, a hundred and fifty-eight, a hundred and sixty-three.
[exhales] And then?
At two this morning the West recorded a hundred and seventy-one. By five it had only eased to a hundred and fifty-four.
So which band is a hundred and seventy-one?

[pause] That's harder to answer than it should be. The agency publishes four hourly bands and puts a number on two of them. Normal is fifty-five and below. Elevated runs fifty-five to a hundred and fifty.
[skeptical] And the band above? Nothing?
No concentration range at all — only a cross-reference to a daily index the country hasn't reached. So the reading passed the top of the only band they quantify, into one that has no number.
What was the forecast saying while this happened?

Thursday evening's advisory forecast a range it called high moderate to mid unhealthy. Same phrase as Monday. Sunday's differed by one word. And both Wednesday's and Thursday's notices said the full extent of the situation could not be determined due to extensive cloud cover.
[thoughtful] They're saying they can't see it. Where's it coming from?

The wrong direction. NASA's detections inside fixed boxes gave six thousand three hundred and forty-one fires over Kalimantan on Wednesday, against two thousand three hundred and sixty-eight over Sumatra.
Nearly three to one, from the east. Which is why Central overtook West.
Different sensor from the regional centre's own series, so the counts aren't comparable — and that centre's numbers are unreachable. Seventh route we've tried.
[sighs] And the Grand Prix opens tonight. What are people actually saying?

That's the part I'd flag. Overnight the argument stopped being about the smoke and became about the measurement — people posting third-party app readings beside the official label. The sharpest line was the shortest: will monitor what they put during the race.
[wry] That's a lot of distrust in nine words.

There's an honest brake on it, though, from the health ministry. Asked in Parliament about fine particulates and lung cancer in people who never smoked, it said the link is real in international studies — but that this is often after long term exposure, and the effect of our periodic haze exposure will only be known much later.
[thoughtful] A ministry saying out loud that it doesn't know yet. Better than a reassuring answer.
France. Thursday was the fourth nationwide day of the school revolt, and the smallest — the interior ministry counted seventy-one thousand five hundred marchers.
Against what on Tuesday?
Two hundred and fifty thousand.
[gasps] A seventy-one per cent collapse in forty-eight hours.

On the day the government gave way. The education minister said three thousand teachers would join within hours; two hours later the prime minister said three thousand and twenty-four. The unions refused and called the next strike for Tuesday.
And the arrests — this is the bit I couldn't get past.
The interior ministry says six thousand one hundred arrested since it began, most under eighteen. The justice ministry says five thousand and sixty, of whom eighty-seven per cent are minors.
[pause] A thousand and forty teenagers apart.

And neither is lying. One counts those seized at the scene; the other those placed in formal custody. It isn't a dispute about facts — it's two ministries measuring different things and both calling it arrests.
What about injuries?

Two hundred and fifteen teenagers, eighty-five school staff, seven hundred and fifteen police. The interior minister has suspended stun grenades for this movement after a fifteen-year-old lost a hand — while conceding only that a police grenade was a strong possibility.
[sighs] A third contested fact in one story. What are the two sides actually arguing about?

A ratio. A student spokesperson said: until we have ten billion euros on the table, we will continue to take action. The same day, the prime minister's own council of twenty-three economists published its first collective note since two thousand and fourteen, calling for a hundred and twenty-five billion of deficit reduction by twenty thirty-two.
[drawn out] Ten billion from the street. A hundred and twenty-five from down the corridor.
And the polling holds both majorities in one sample. Seventy-two per cent think the demands legitimate; fifty-five per cent think the protests should stop.
What's the sceptic's case?

It cuts for the students. French fifteen-year-olds scored forty-three points lower in reading last year than in twenty fifteen — the largest fall in the OECD. And the cost is real too: twenty-four schools shut for weeks, thirty thousand pupils, twenty to thirty million euros.
[thoughtful] Both true at once. That seems to be today's shape.
One more from that desk. The Makkah defence pact activated on Monday — the three signatories agreed on the rapid deployment of agreed forces and capabilities.
And by Thursday?

Turkey's foreign minister said on television that it is not an attack agreement. Pakistan's military spokesman confirmed its forces are already there — and its information ministry, the same day, called a report that Pakistani jets were flying against the Houthis fake and fabricated.
[scoffs] Confirmation and denial inside one day.

And the air campaign has four counts. Three hundred and twenty-four high-value targets from the coalition spokesman. Eighty-two destroyed on Thursday from the coalition itself. A hundred and fifty-six Saudi strikes from the Houthi spokesman. And more than a thousand airstrikes from a Chinese researcher on Beijing's own broadcaster.
[deadpan] Twelve times the coalition's own figure. Another week, another set of numbers that don't meet.
Which is the bridge to the money. Exactly one scheduled American release landed all week, so the long end was priced by something else.
By what?
Houthi strikes on two Saudi airports took Brent up three point seven one per cent in a single session, to a hundred and three dollars ninety-two.
So yields rose.

They fell. The ten-year went from five point three one to five point two two, the real yield from two point nine five to two point eight seven, and breakeven inflation moved two point three six to two point three five across the whole week.
[curious] Oil up four, yields down, inflation compensation flat. The bond market didn't read the oil as inflation.

It read it as risk. And the term premium set a new high — the New York Fed's ten-year estimate reached nought point nine eight four eight on Tuesday, against the nought point nine six two one we printed yesterday. That moves the record back to June twenty fourteen.
Here's what I want explained. You said the rally was mostly real yields.
Eighty-nine per cent real, measured one way. But the term-structure model says it happened only because the expected-rate path fell faster than the premium climbed.
[thoughtful] So the same move decomposes two opposite ways in one week.
Different cuts, not a contradiction. But print one without the other and you've misled someone.
Name the regime.

Tightening — and this is the one most easily got wrong. On the sixteenth of September the committee raised a quarter point, twelve to nothing. The minutes say inflation remains elevated, and that Treasury supply was contributing to higher term premiums and Treasury yields.
What did Singapore do?

Took it squarely. The index fell three point four nine per cent, a two-day loss of five per cent, with the three banks — over a quarter of the index — down between four point eight and five point three.
And next week?
Wednesday brings the policy statement, the Macroeconomic Review, third-quarter output and American consumer prices. All on one day.
[wry] So clear your Wednesday.
And this is market explanation, not investment advice.
Technology. Samsung had a quarter.
A record one. Operating profit around a hundred and seven point four trillion won, up seven hundred and eighty-three per cent. And the preliminary filing carries no segment breakdown at all.
So every explanation is somebody's estimate. How far apart?
One outlet puts the finished-products division at about a two-trillion-won loss. Another reports a securities-firm estimate that the mobile division's loss could reach nineteen trillion.
[gasps] Seventeen trillion won of disagreement about a number nobody has.

About thirteen billion US dollars of it. And the phone division bleeds for the reason the memory division doesn't — twelve-gigabyte mobile memory is up a hundred and seventy-five per cent on the year, and Samsung sells that part to itself.
On the same day as the record?
A Korean outlet reported the mobile division asking partners for twenty to thirty per cent supply cuts, under the headline: there is no profit even if we sell.
[deadpan] Record quarter. No profit even if we sell. Anything for the home lab?

The multi-GPU expert cache merged Thursday. The author measured decode going from thirty-four to sixty-four tokens a second on two cards — but prompt processing fell twenty-seven per cent on the same run, and two independent testers measured it slower overall.
How much slower?
One reported generation falling from thirty-three tokens a second to sixteen, on a different model. No maintainer answered him on the page.
[skeptical] Right. And The Kit?
Bose opened preorders on a wired earbud. Ninety-nine US dollars, noise cancelling with nothing to charge. The page says, in three words: no charging needed.
And?
Scroll down the same page and the specification table says rechargeable, yes. And charging accessory included, yes.
[laughs] On the same page?

In two countries, unreconciled in both. And no attenuation figure in decibels, for a product sold on noise cancelling — and no power draw, which is the one number that tells you what it costs your phone.
Can we buy it here?

Not listed in Singapore at all. And today's Atelier is mattresses, where the headline is ownership. Vispring of Plymouth, the American houses Kluft and Aireloom, a British retailer, and Marshall Mattress of Toronto — whose eighteen ninety-nine pocket-coil patent Vispring was founded to license.
Let me guess. All one company.
One Madrid company.
[amused] Four heritages, one balance sheet.

And the coil count on the label is, in the specialists' own words, among the worst possible ways to buy a mattress. The figure that would tell you something is the weight of the steel, which is almost never printed.
What's the Singapore catch?
A warranty. The local latex specialist's own terms exclude humidity damage and will not cover mildew stains.
[exhales] In Singapore. Quite an exclusion.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
What is it?
Ten-metre target shooting. It starts with two numbers. The ten-ring on an air-pistol target is eleven point five millimetres across.
Fine. Small.
On an air-rifle target it is nought point five millimetres. A printed dot, thinner than the pencil you'd mark it with.
[gasps] Half a millimetre? At ten metres, standing?

Unsupported. Scoring is by outward gauge, so the pellet counts if its hole breaks the line — which makes the real tolerance one point seven two arc-minutes. A ten point nine means the pellet's centre arrived within a quarter of a millimetre of the middle.
[drawn out] That's absurd. Why is it so hard?

A Spanish group measured it. Tracking three hundred and sixty shots from one elite shooter, the aim point moves at a hundred and eight millimetres a second in the final second before release. The gun never stops — it travels about the width of the target card every second.
So it's about holding still.

[pause] That's what everyone teaches. That paper found otherwise in its elite subject — stability of hold explained between two and three per cent, and it concluded that hold does not seem to be a determining factor of the score.
Against what the field believes?
Thirty-three per cent of score variance in pistol, fifty-four in rifle, in the literature it cites. One shooter isn't a sample, and the authors say so.
[curious] Can you actually do this in Singapore?

You can, and the law is the interesting part. An air pistol here is a gun. The police licensing guideline sets six conditions and the fifth is flat — all guns must be stored in the approved armoury at the shooting club.
So you never take it home. Ever.

Which inverts the order of buying. A beginner takes a licence to use the club's pool guns. Membership from seventy-eight Singapore dollars a year, and the six-lesson basic course is two hundred and ninety-seven seventy-five.
That is much less than I expected.
Club first, licence second, gun last or never. And if you do buy, the real entry is a match pistol at about fifteen hundred US dollars, climbing fast to three and a half thousand.
Does any of it make you shoot better?
That's the honest part, and it comes from owners. On choosing between flagships, one writes: all the top guns will be better and more accurate than the human at the other end.
[laughs] Well, that settles that.
And another, on a custom grip he waited months and three hundred and fifty euros for — it hasn't improved my scores at all, but looks good.
[chuckles] I love this sport already. What's the obsession this month?

Grips. From the first of July the rules fixed three angles, and shooters across the world began taking a rasp to walnut they'd waited six months for. One man reshaped nine pistols in about three hours.
[amused] Did anyone explain why?

Nobody answered that one either. And the real constraint here isn't money — the national competition has gone from eleven events last year to seven, with the longer distances now closed to everyone outside the national team.
Why?
Lane limitations. In their own words.
Culture desk, quickly.
Sorkin's sequel opens today. Rotten Tomatoes has it at sixty-one per cent from a hundred and twenty critics; Metacritic has fifty-three from forty-five.
Which is right?
Neither, in the sense you mean — they measure different things, and the counts differ by a factor of two point seven. And there's no box office yet. Every figure circulating is a forecast.
[wry] We learned that lesson two issues ago.

We did. But last weekend's actuals have the better fact. An Indian sequel opened on five hundred and forty-one screens and took five thousand and sixty-four dollars a screen, against two thousand and twenty-five for a wide release on three and a half thousand.
One-seventh of the footprint, two and a half times the yield. Watches?

Bremont announced a ceramic diver. Three magazines printed that it's limited to two hundred and fifty pieces. The maker's own shop prints no limitation at all — on a page where the cheaper white model says limited to a hundred and fifty.
[scoffs] So the dearest watch is the one they won't call scarce.

Four hundred and fifty dollars above the limited one. Family desk: Singapore's paediatric advice says under-twelves should avoid caffeine, and twelve to eighteens may have up to a hundred milligrams a day.
So a child who turned twelve this year crossed a line.
In July, and nothing announced it. The ministry also said it collects no data on children seeking medical attention for caffeine, and that there is no recognised health-based guidance to publish.
[thoughtful] Unusually honest.

And the counterweight on the facing page. Across three hundred and fifty-five thousand adolescents, technology use explains at most nought point four per cent of the variation in well-being. A larger study put it in the moment — when people felt social media was affecting them, well-being dropped two per cent against their own average.
And the comparison?
Music, plus eight. Relaxing, plus six. Studying — minus seven.
[laughs] Homework is three times worse than Instagram.
By the users' own reckoning. Fitness: the chronotype claim finally got its randomised trial. A hundred and eight adults, twelve weeks, lifting at their profiled best hour or their worst.
And?
Nought point nought six newtons per kilogram, with an interval running from minus nought point seven six to plus nought point eight eight.
[deadpan] So, nothing.

The authors' words: aligning training with an individual's peak performance time of day did not enhance skeletal muscle adaptations. And there's a bookkeeping catch — the paper reports fourteen per cent dropout in the peak group, then two sentences later lists that group's departures as eight women and three men.
Eleven. Out of how many?
Forty-four.
[pause] That's twenty-five per cent, not fourteen.

It doesn't touch the finding, which is null either way. But it's the paper that will be cited to close the question. And one for the Diary: every day of the November sumo in Fukuoka is gone, and the association says no tickets are sold on the day.
When's the next chance?

Tokyo in January, advance sales on the fifth of December. Diarise the on-sale, not the tournament. And Kyoto's maples peak on the eleventh of December this year — book late November for red leaves and you arrive two weeks early.
All right. The Maldives.

[pause] The central bank publishes a spreadsheet. One column records official reserve assets, month by month. January, one thousand and twenty-six million dollars. February, one thousand two hundred and seventy-two. March, one thousand three hundred and thirty-two.
And April?
Seven hundred and eighteen.
[exhales] Six hundred million dollars in thirty days.

By July it was six hundred and thirty-eight — the lowest in the published series. And it wasn't a run. A five-hundred-million-dollar sukuk and a four-hundred-million currency swap both fell due that month. A bill arrived and was paid, in full and on time.
So where's the story?

In what the state had said eight weeks earlier. On the fifth of February the president told parliament that gross reserves stood in excess of one point one three billion dollars, representing the highest level in the history of our nation — and that of the sukuk, the hundred and fifty million dollar portion would be discharged using the reserves.
[drawn out] A hundred and fifty million. And the drawdown was six hundred and fourteen.
Four times the portion he named.
So what does a country do when it runs out of dollars?

First it legislates them home. Resorts were already made to convert either five hundred US dollars per tourist or twenty per cent of monthly gross. Four hundred and ninety-two million reached the central bank last year. Then on the first of September the quota doubled to forty per cent, and the per-tourist option was deleted.
But that only moves dollars that already exist.

[warmly] That's exactly the point. New dollars need a new export, and the Maldives has nothing left to add — tourism, fish, and a constitution that forbids foreign ownership of any part of its territory.
So?
So it manufactured territory. Since December twenty twenty-three, roughly eleven hundred hectares have been dredged out of a lagoon south of the capital.
Give me the scale.

Malé is two hundred and eight hectares carrying a hundred and thirty-seven thousand residents — six hundred and sixty people per hectare, among the densest ground on earth. The new land is nearly twice the entire built capital region.
And the terms?
Here I have to be careful. The developer's own release says that upon each transfer, whether through sale or inheritance, a new leasehold term of up to ninety-nine years will commence.
[curious] And the constitutional cap is ninety-nine years.
So every sale restarts the clock. No single lease breaks the ceiling, and the tenure never ends.
That's a constitutional limit defeated by arithmetic.

That's the reading — and here's the warning I'd rather print than the thesis. That sentence appears in the developer's international release. It was absent from the ministry's own Maldivian version. And the attorney-general said on the record that so far only a letter of intent has been signed.
[thoughtful] So the load-bearing fact lives in a press release, not a contract.
The governing act is still being drafted and the agreement is unpublished.
Then what can we stand behind?

That almost every figure attached to the scheme exists in more than one official version. The project is worth twelve billion in the developer's release and twenty billion when ministers describe it. The reclamation is eleven hundred and fifty-three hectares in the original plan, a thousand and nine on the housing corporation's reckoning, about eleven hundred from the finance minister.
[sighs] Three numbers for a piece of ground somebody dredged.

And the state's ten-year take is more than eleven billion according to one minister and more than three billion according to another. There's a Maldivian precedent too, and it cuts the other way — in twenty fifteen the constitution was amended to allow outright foreign freehold on reclaimed sites, and in April twenty nineteen it was repealed unanimously. No land was ever sold under it.
So they've announced something like this before and not done it.

And the number that would settle the argument is the one nobody publishes. The central bank reports gross reserves; the usable figure, historically much smaller, appears nowhere. And the IMF has published no Maldives staff report since May twenty twenty-four.
[pause] So the institution whose job is to say has gone quiet.

The honest version is narrower than the dramatic one, and more interesting. A state met a scheduled bill on time and it cost half its reserves. It responded by compelling its resorts to hand over twice as many dollars, and by preparing to sell ground that did not exist three years ago to buyers who cannot legally own it.
[thoughtful] Treating its own exchange rate as a construction project.
That's the line. Whether the lease really renews forever isn't yet knowable, because the contract doesn't exist.
[warmly] And when it does, that's the sentence to read first. Good place to stop.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
